cardTitle: Traveling for the holidays with medications

Travel

Traveling for the holidays with medications: a pharmacist's checklist.

Flying out of Orlando or driving to see family in December? A little planning keeps your medicines, and your pet's, from becoming the stressful part of the trip.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 25, 2026

1. Refill early

  • Check your supply two weeks before you leave. Count what you have, and compare it to the days you'll be away plus a few extra in case of delays.
  • Call in refills early. Pharmacies are busy before the holidays, and a prescription that's out of refills needs your prescriber's approval, which can take a few days. We contact your prescriber for you.
  • Need it sooner than usual? Insurance plans limit how early you can refill. Some allow an early fill for travel. Ask us and we'll check your plan.
  • Think about 90-day supplies. For medicines you take every day, a 90-day supply means fewer trips and less chance of running short while you're away. Ask about med sync too, so all your refills are ready on one day.

2. Pack it right

  • Keep medicines in your carry-on, not in checked luggage, where bags can be lost or delayed. On road trips, don't leave medicines in a hot or freezing car.
  • Use the original labeled containers when you can. TSA doesn't require them, but labels make it easy to show what a medicine is, and some states and countries have their own rules. If you use a pill organizer, bring the labeled bottles or a copy of the labels too.
  • Liquid medicines larger than 3.4 ounces are allowed in your carry-on in reasonable amounts. Tell the TSA officer at the start of screening so they can screen them separately. Ice packs for medicines that need to stay cold are allowed too.
  • Bring a written medication list with each medicine's name, strength and directions, plus your allergies, your prescriber's name and number, and your pharmacy's number. A photo on your phone works too.
  • Pet medicines count. If your dog or cat is coming along, pack their medicines in your carry-on with the label and your veterinarian's phone number.

3. Handle time zones

Flying from Florida to the West Coast puts you three hours behind. For many once-a-day medicines, taking a dose a little early or late on travel day isn't a problem. Some medicines are more time-sensitive, such as insulin, birth control pills, seizure medicines and certain heart medicines. If you take any of these, ask your pharmacist or prescriber for a plan before you leave, including how to shift back when you get home.

4. If you forget a dose

Check the directions on the label or the leaflet that came with your medicine; many say what to do about a missed dose. For many medicines, you take it when you remember unless it's almost time for the next one. Don't double up unless your prescriber or pharmacist tells you to. When in doubt, call us. A pharmacist answers.

5. If you run out while away

  • Call us first. We'll look at your prescription and refills and help you find the fastest option.
  • Use a local pharmacy. If you have refills left, a pharmacy where you're staying can contact us to transfer the prescription. Bring your medication list or a labeled bottle.
  • Call your prescriber if you're out of refills. They may be able to send a new prescription to a pharmacy near you.
Don't wait it out. Stopping some medicines suddenly can be risky. If you run out of a medicine you take every day, call your prescriber or a local pharmacist the same day. For chest pain, trouble breathing, a seizure or a severe reaction, call 911.

Your quick checklist

  1. Count your supply two weeks before you go.
  2. Order refills and ask about early or 90-day fills.
  3. Pack everything, including pet medicines, in your carry-on.
  4. Bring labeled bottles and a written medication list.
  5. Make a plan for time-sensitive medicines and time zones.
  6. Save our number: 407-977-9779.

You can refill by phone, by text, online or with our MobileScripts app, and we'll text you when your prescription is ready.

Easy refills Call 407-977-9779

Common questions

Do my medications have to be in the original bottles to fly?

TSA doesn't require it, but original labeled containers make screening and any questions easier, and some states and countries have their own rules. At least bring copies of your labels and a medication list.

Can I bring liquid medicine through airport security?

Yes. Liquid medicines larger than 3.4 ounces are allowed in your carry-on in reasonable amounts. Tell the TSA officer at the start of screening.

Can you ship my refill to where I'm visiting?

We ship to Florida, Maine and Colorado. Elsewhere, refill before you leave, or call us and we'll help a local pharmacy get your prescription.

This article is general information and not medical advice. Check current TSA rules before you fly, and ask your prescriber or pharmacist about your own medicines.
